title: Prove the Mark III's learning rule on a seven-day watering curve
tier_reason: New code behind a test and a demo; git reverts it. The choice it settles (REINFORCE trace vs evolutionary strategies) is an engineering call the design leaves to the spike.
ask: The design in docs/design/06 ('The ladder's third rung') proposes a linear softmax policy (103 inputs x 6 actions) trained by REINFORCE with an eligibility trace, updated once at the day turn, with exploration drawn from SimRng.stateless so replays recompute it. Prove it learns the v1 watering job, or show that evolutionary strategies does better at the same storage cost. This is the first cut of the D-2 spike. Reward is +1 per tile made wet and 0 otherwise (Q-96, ruled) — no shaping penalties; if learning is slow, that is exploration's and the baseline's problem, not the reward's.
first_action: Write tools/demo_learning_robot.gd on the pattern of tools/demo_robot_value.gd: one seed, a staged field with dry wettable soil, a Mark III (or a test species with the same observation and action set) run for seven in-game days; print per-day score; assert the curve rises and that two runs are byte-identical. Keep every array JSON-plain in the actor's extra. Warrants the stronger model.
source_message: CEO, 2026-09-09, chief of staff session: v0.2.1 is the Mark III, the robot that learns by reinforcement (P-14).
result: Landed on main (commit 0648e9f merged): tools/demo_learning_robot.gd and test_learning_robot (7 assertions). Seed 20260909, seven days: 1, 9, 3, 10, 9, 10, 9 thirsty squares watered; two runs identical weight for weight; days 5-7 beat days 1-3. Unit 2356, integration 650 (671 after the panel), robot session and gateway check green. Two findings, reported not hidden: (1) the night rule mismatches credit and baseline — acc credits each decision with the rewards after it, baseline·trace subtracts the whole day's mean from every decision — so learning is weak (24 seeds: 8.6 vs 7.1 a day against no learning) and the rate had to drop to 0.02; the fix is a state-dependent baseline, queued to a worker. (2) The plan's staging measured nothing: a zero-weight robot leaves a 6x4 block within a minute of random walking; the demo pens it in a 9x4 fenced paddock. That is a design question for the CEO (Q-99). Chief of staff verified: ran both suites on main after the merge. Follow-up landed (commit 25d26a5 merged as 5b80ffc): the baseline mismatch is fixed with a state-dependent baseline (a third trace scaled by the fraction of the meter left), LEARN_RATE 0.03 from a sweep of six rates over 24 seeds each; days 5-7 average 9.1 squares against 6.6 with the night switched off, 20 of 24 weeks rose, and it holds at 9.2 on day 20 where the old rule sank below the control. Unit 2357, integration 671, robot session and gateway green.

follow_ups.title: Give the learning rule a per-situation baseline so credit and comparison line up
follow_ups.first_action: In the night update in the Mark III policy code, replace the single day-mean baseline with a per-decision state-dependent baseline (learned value estimate over the same 103 inputs), then re-run the 24-seed comparison and report the new tiles-per-day against the 8.6 vs 7.1 figure.
follow_ups.why: The demo's own finding: acc credits each decision with what followed it while the baseline subtracts one day-wide number, so the signal is weak and the rate had to be crippled to 0.02.

follow_ups.title: Measure evolutionary strategies against the same weight budget
follow_ups.first_action: Add a tools/demo_es_robot.gd that trains the same 103x6 linear policy by evolutionary strategies (population perturbations scored on a full day, seeded from SimRng.stateless), run it on seed 20260909 for seven days in the same fenced paddock, and print the same day-by-day table so the two rules can be read side by side.
follow_ups.why: The D-2 spike asked for REINFORCE or evidence that evolutionary strategies beats it at the same storage cost, and only the first half was answered.

follow_ups.title: Design the fence a player buys to pen a learning robot
follow_ups.first_action: Draft the paddock in docs/design/06: a fence bought from the shop and placed on tiles, what it costs, how big a first one is, what the robot does when it reaches an edge, and what the player sees that explains why the robot is confined. Keep v1 deliberately limited per the standing rule and file open questions to DESIGNER_QUEUE.
follow_ups.why: The demo's paddock was a measurement fixture; accepting the recommendation turns it into a real thing players build, and that needs a design before any code.

follow_ups.title: Record the paddock ruling against Q-99 and close the item
follow_ups.first_action: Annotate Q-99 in docs/DESIGNER_QUEUE.md with the CEO's ruling that learning robots are confined by a player-built fence, add the matching entry to docs/DECISION_LOG.md, and set the ruling record in hq/data/rulings/ to integrated.
follow_ups.why: The decision inbox has to reflect what this acceptance settled, or the same question comes back at the next spike.

recommend.question: While a Mark III is learning, does it stay inside a fence you put up, or roam the whole farm?
recommend.answer: Make the fence real — a paddock bought in the shop that the robot learns inside, and keep the open farm for robots that have already learned.
recommend.why: A fresh robot wanders off a small plot within a minute, so without a fence its first days teach it nothing and read to the player as a broken machine rather than a learning one.
recommend.instead: Let it roam from day one and solve the wandering inside the learning rule instead, which keeps the world unchanged and adds nothing for the player to buy or place, but leaves early days looking like a malfunction.
